AN EMPRESS, A FOOTBALL GAME HIJACKED BY HEIDI, A ROBOT ON THE MOON, A UFO OVER ALASKA & A REVOLUTION THAT TURNED VELVET INTO HISTORY!  🫣

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

THE WEIRDEST EVENTS IN HISTORY 🤯

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

STRANGER THAN FICTION — NOVEMBER 17 EDITION

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🕒 ESTIMATED READING TIME: 12 MINUTES

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🗺️ CONSPECTUS

📜 EPIGRAPH — A little truth to set the tone.

🎬 INTRO — Five stories. One very strange date.

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY — Test your instincts.

⭐️ MAIN EVENTS — Five moments when history got spectacularly weird.

🎙️ HARVEY’S CORNER — The rest of the story.

⚖️ CLOSING — The day, considered.

✅ QUIZ ANSWER — The answer revealed.

🍬 CANDY — One last sweet bite, with a look at tomorrow.

💋 SEND-OFF — Pass the madness along.

📣 THERE’S MORE HISTORY WAITING! — The daily lineup.

📚 SOURCES & FURTHER READING — Follow the evidence.

✒️ PUDD’NHEAD WILSON HAS THE LAST WORD — Mark Twain gets the final say.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

📜 EPIGRAPH

“Truth is stranger than fiction, but it is because Fiction is obliged to stick to possibilities; Truth isn't.” ~ Mark Twain, Following the Equator (1897).  ☄️

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🎬 INTRO

What do an empress with her own personal armada, a football game ruined by a little girl, and a machine out for a leisurely stroll on the Moon have in common? Besides a complete absence of adult supervision, they all share a date that clearly never got the memo about behaving normally.

But wait, there’s more, as the infomercials say. A crew of seasoned airline pilots meets something above the last frontier that refuses to fit into any explanation, and trust me, they tried them all. Thousands of students take to the streets and help change the fate of an entire nation, because apparently that’s what happens when young people get fed up and decide they've had enough. And somewhere far from all the chaos, a young mechanic with more grit than cash is about to start a journey that will change transportation forever. Broke, stubborn, and unstoppable, which is a terrible combination for the rest of us.

A television network commits a blunder so spectacular it deserves its own parade. November 17 didn’t just show up; it brought a whole cast of lunatics, geniuses, and unanswered questions.

Five extraordinary events. One remarkable inventor. And enough historical mischief to make fiction pack its bags and go home in shame.

Cue the chaos. Let's roll. 💥

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY

On November 17, 1968, millions of American television viewers missed one of the most extraordinary finishes in professional football history.

What caused them to miss it?

[A] A nationwide electrical blackout.

[B] A children's movie replaced the live broadcast before the game ended.

[C] A technical failure destroyed the television transmission.

[D] The network accidentally broadcast a different game.

👇 (Answer at the end of the issue.)

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

⭐️ MAIN EVENTS

🚢 1869 — THE CANAL, THE EMPRESS & THE FLOATING PARADE

November 17, 1869 | Port Said, Egypt

After ten years of construction, the Suez Canal was officially inaugurated, connecting the Mediterranean and Red Seas and transforming the route between Europe and Asia.

The ceremony was an international spectacle attended by approximately 6,000 guests, including monarchs, diplomats, aristocrats, and cultural figures. Among the most prominent was Empress Eugénie of France, wife of Napoleon III, who arrived aboard the imperial yacht L’Aigle, which was meant to lead the procession of vessels into the new waterway.

Egypt’s Khedive Ismail had invested heavily in presenting his country as a modern power. The canal was both an engineering achievement and a declaration of commercial ambition: ships could now avoid the lengthy journey around Africa’s southern tip.

The project had required enormous excavation and difficult working conditions. Its opening changed international transportation and made the waterway one of the world’s most strategically important passages.

🧩 TRIVIA: The project required the removal of approximately 74 million cubic metres (96.8 million cubic yards) of soil. Its execution cost reached 433 million francs, about twice the initial estimate.

🌀 OBSCURE: L’Aigle was supposed to lead the ceremonial procession, but Captain George Nares, commanding HMS Newport, had other ideas. Under cover of total darkness, without lights, he maneuvered his ship through the waiting vessels and made it through the canal ahead of the imperial yacht. Although the maneuver earned him an official reprimand, it also gave the British commander a rather cheeky place in the canal's history.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The canal changed the geography of commerce. Sometimes human ambition begins by refusing to accept the boundaries nature appears to have established.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

📺 1968 — THE DAY HEIDI STOLE A FOOTBALL GAME

November 17, 1968 | Oakland, California, United States

Imagine watching an important football game, waiting for the final seconds, and suddenly finding yourself watching a children's movie instead. Millions of American viewers experienced precisely that.

The New York Jets were playing the Oakland Raiders. With 65 seconds remaining, the Jets led 32–29. NBC had scheduled a television adaptation of Heidi to begin at a fixed time, and the network switched away from the game.

There was just one problem: the game wasn't over.
Oakland scored a touchdown to take the lead. Then the Jets fumbled the ensuing kickoff, and Oakland recovered and scored again. Two touchdowns in the final nine seconds gave the Raiders a 43–32 victory.

Millions of viewers missed the finish. NBC's telephone lines were overwhelmed by furious callers, and the network apologized. The incident became known as the Heidi Game and helped change how broadcasters handled live sporting events.

🧩 TRIVIA: The game featured ten future Pro Football Hall of Famers. It was already a remarkable contest before the broadcast disaster made it legendary.

🐶 SPOT: The incident became a lasting lesson in live television scheduling. NBC's predetermined programming plan had taken priority over the final seconds of a major sporting event. After the uproar, broadcasters took steps to ensure that scheduled entertainment would not again automatically displace a live game.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A network can control its programming schedule, but it cannot control what happens in the final seconds of a football game.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🌕 1970 — THE FIRST WHEELED VISITOR TO ANOTHER WORLD

November 17, 1970 | Mare Imbrium, Moon

A Soviet spacecraft delivered Lunokhod 1 to the lunar surface, making it the first successful wheeled rover to operate on another celestial body.

The Luna 17 mission landed in the Sea of Rains. After descending from its landing platform, the eight-wheeled vehicle rolled onto the Moon and began photographing the landscape, examining the soil, and conducting scientific experiments.

Operators on Earth guided the rover across unfamiliar terrain, using images and data sent back from the lunar surface. The task demanded careful remote control over a vast distance, with communication delays making the work anything but simple.

Lunokhod's planned operational life was three lunar days—about 21 Earth days. Instead, it functioned for 322 days, travelled approximately 10.5 kilometres, and sent back thousands of images and valuable scientific information.

The little machine helped turn the Moon from a place humans could visit into a place robotic explorers could investigate.

🧩 TRIVIA: Lunokhod 1 weighed approximately 756 kilograms and had eight independently driven wheels. Its design allowed it to negotiate obstacles and travel across terrain that would have challenged a conventional vehicle.

🔑 ESOTERIC: The rover carried a French-built laser reflector containing 14 prisms. Scientists on Earth later used laser pulses directed at the reflector to measure the Earth–Moon distance with remarkable precision. A small robotic explorer was helping measure the distance between two worlds.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Exploration does not always require a human being to take the first step. Sometimes a machine can go where its creators cannot—and send back knowledge for the next journey.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🛸 1986 — THE UFO THAT FOLLOWED A JUMBO JET

November 17, 1986 | Above Alaska, United States

Commercial pilots are trained to recognize aircraft, weather phenomena, and potential hazards. But what happens when experienced flight crew members report something they cannot identify?

The crew of Japan Airlines Flight 1628 encountered an extraordinary situation while flying a Boeing 747 cargo aircraft over Alaska. Captain Kenju Terauchi and his two fellow crew members reported unusual lights accompanying their aircraft.

The flight was travelling from Iceland toward Tokyo, with a stop in Anchorage. Over Alaska, the crew observed lights that appeared to move alongside the jet. Terauchi described two smaller illuminated objects and another enormous object that seemed to follow the aircraft.

The crew reported that the lights remained visible as the aircraft changed course and contacted air traffic controllers. The incident attracted attention because the witnesses were professional pilots, not casual observers.

The Federal Aviation Administration investigated, interviewing the crew and examining radar records and communications. The investigation did not establish that an unidentified craft had accompanied the Boeing 747.

The FAA could not confirm what the crew had witnessed. The pilots’ account nevertheless became one of the most discussed aviation UFO incidents of the 1980s.

🧩 TRIVIA: All three crew members—Captain Terauchi, First Officer Takanori Tamefuji, and Flight Engineer Yoshio Tsukuda—were interviewed by FAA investigators. The agency’s records included pilot interviews, controller communications, and radar information.

🕵️ MYSTERY: What did the crew actually see? The crew were experienced professionals, and FAA investigators found them rational and sober. The FAA still could not confirm that an unidentified craft accompanied the jet. The radar return that seemed to show a second object was a split return from the 747 itself, but that explains the radar image, not the lights the crew saw.

Skeptic Philip Klass argued that the lights were the planets Jupiter and Mars low on the horizon, possibly distorted by ice crystals in the cold air. The crew rejected that explanation, and the FAA never settled the question.

What is known: three pilots reported something they could not identify. What is uncertain: whether it was misidentified planets, an atmospheric effect, or something else.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: An unexplained sighting is not proof of an extraterrestrial visitor. A careful investigation distinguishes what witnesses reported, what instruments recorded, and what the evidence can establish.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🕯️ 1989 — THE VELVET REVOLUTION BEGINS

November 17, 1989 | Prague, Czechoslovakia

Some revolutions begin with armies and declarations of war. Others begin with students carrying banners and hoping their country might someday become free.

Thousands of students gathered in Prague to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the Nazi suppression of Czech universities. In November 1939, occupation authorities had closed the universities, arrested students, sent more than a thousand to concentration camps, and executed nine student leaders.

The 1989 demonstration was initially authorized as a commemorative march. But the peaceful procession became an expression of opposition to the communist government. Police blocked the route and attacked demonstrators on Národní Street. Hundreds were injured.

The crackdown shocked the public and helped ignite a much wider movement. Students organized strikes, theater performers joined the demonstrations, and citizens increasingly filled the streets. The Civic Forum emerged as an opposition movement, and negotiations led to the end of communist rule.

By December, playwright and dissident Václav Havel had become president. The largely peaceful transition became known as the Velvet Revolution.

🧩 TRIVIA: November 17 was designated International Students' Day in 1941, commemorating the Nazi crackdown on Czech students in 1939.

🐶 SPOT: The police assault did not immediately overthrow the government. Its importance lay in the public reaction: a student protest became a national movement as ordinary citizens recognized the attack as an assault on their own freedom.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A government can suppress a demonstration, but it cannot always suppress the determination that brought people into the streets.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🎙️ HARVEY’S CORNER

🔧 SOICHIRO HONDA — THE BOY WHO TURNED A BICYCLE INTO A DREAM

Good day, everybody.

Some people see a machine and admire what it can do. Others immediately wonder how it works—and how to make it work better. Soichiro Honda belonged firmly in the second category.

Born November 17, 1906, in Komyo Village, Japan, he was the eldest son of a blacksmith and a weaver. His father, Gihei, was skilled at working with metal and also operated a bicycle shop. His mother, Mika, was an accomplished weaver. Their household was not wealthy, but practical craftsmanship was part of everyday life.

Honda's fascination with machinery began early. An automobile passing through his village made a lasting impression. He never forgot the smell of its oil. At fifteen, he left home for Tokyo and became an apprentice at the Art Shokai automobile repair shop.

He learned by doing: repairing engines, working on vehicles, and developing a reputation for mechanical ingenuity. But he was interested in more than repairing other people's machines.

While still an apprentice, he helped his employers, the Sakakibara brothers, build a racing car called the Curtiss. Its engine had originally powered an American Curtiss Jenny biplane and was fitted into the chassis of a Mitchell automobile. On November 23, 1924, the machine won the Fifth Japan Motor Car Championship, with Honda serving as its riding mechanic.

Imagine that: a teenager helping put an aircraft engine into a car and then taking it racing. Apparently, ordinary transportation had never held much appeal for him.

In 1928, Honda completed his apprenticeship and was entrusted with opening an Art Shokai branch in Hamamatsu. He eventually established his own manufacturing venture, Tokai Seiki, with a determination to produce automobile piston rings.

But his first attempts were anything but successful.

His early piston rings suffered from serious technical problems. Honda discovered that practical mechanical ability alone wasn't enough to master the science of manufacturing. Rather than pretend he knew everything, he enrolled in technical studies to improve his understanding of metallurgy.

The effort paid off, but the road remained difficult. When he submitted fifty piston rings to Toyota for quality inspection, only three met the required standards.

Three out of fifty.

Most people might have considered that a reason to abandon the project. Honda considered it a reason to learn more. He visited universities and steelmaking companies, studied manufacturing techniques, and kept experimenting until he could produce components that met the necessary standards.

His company eventually became a major supplier, employing more than 2,000 people at its height.

Then came the war.

Air raids destroyed Tokai Seiki's Yamashita plant, and an earthquake in January 1945 brought down another factory. The business Honda had worked so hard to build was devastated. He eventually sold his interest in the company and began considering what to do next.

Postwar Japan faced enormous shortages, including a desperate need for affordable transportation. Bicycles were among the most important means of getting around, but even those could be difficult to use when carrying heavy loads.

Honda saw an opportunity.

In September 1946, he established the Honda Technical Research Institute. Around that time, he encountered a small surplus engine originally designed to power a wireless radio generator for the former Imperial Japanese Army.

An idea immediately came to him: why not use the engine to power a bicycle?

He acquired approximately 500 of the engines and began adapting them for civilian transportation.

But he didn't simply bolt an engine onto a bicycle and send it out the door. His first experimental arrangement used a friction roller against the front wheel, but the poor-quality tires of the period wore out quickly. He abandoned that approach and developed a more practical belt-driven arrangement.

There was even a wonderfully improvised touch: one early prototype used a Japanese hot-water bottle as its fuel tank.

That's ingenuity with whatever happens to be lying around!

Honda also insisted on quality. He dismantled, refined, and reassembled each engine, then tested the finished bicycle before it reached a customer. The resulting motorized bicycles became popular, offering people a relatively inexpensive way to travel.

But Honda knew the supply of surplus engines wouldn't last forever. He began developing an engine of his own, and in November 1947 introduced the A-Type auxiliary bicycle engine, his first original product.

In September 1948, he founded Honda Motor Co., Ltd. with Takeo Fujisawa, a business partner whose commercial and organizational abilities complemented Honda's engineering imagination.

It was a partnership that mattered enormously. Honda brought technical creativity and an appetite for experimentation; Fujisawa helped build the business capable of turning those ideas into a lasting enterprise.

The company grew from its humble beginnings in Hamamatsu into one of the world's leading motorcycle manufacturers. It later expanded into automobiles and international motorsport, earning a global reputation for engineering, performance, and innovation.

Honda eventually retired from the company's presidency but remained an influential figure. He died on August 5, 1991, aged 84.

Consider the journey: a blacksmith's son leaves home as a teenager, becomes a mechanic, helps build an aircraft-engine racing car, struggles with manufacturing failures, studies metallurgy, loses the factories he worked so hard to establish, and starts again by adapting surplus engines to bicycles.

That is not a conventional corporate success story. It is perseverance with a toolbox.

And perhaps the most remarkable part is that Honda never seemed satisfied with simply making something work. He wanted to understand why it worked, how it could work better, and how it could make life easier for somebody else.

The boy who once watched an automobile pass through his village helped build a company whose machines would eventually travel around the world.

And now, you know the rest of the story.

—— ❧ ——

NOTICE & TRIBUTE: “Harvey’s Corner” is an original historical feature inspired by the storytelling tradition of legendary radio broadcaster Paul Harvey (1918–2009). This independent editorial homage is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by the Paul Harvey estate or ABC Radio.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

⚖️ CLOSING

November 17 reminds us that history rarely follows a predictable script.

The Suez Canal reshaped global commerce. The Heidi Game showed how one scheduling decision could become a national television disaster. Lunokhod 1 proved that machines could explore another world. The Alaska encounter remains a debated aviation mystery, while the Velvet Revolution demonstrated how students and ordinary citizens could help transform a nation.

And Soichiro Honda's life offers a lesson of its own: failure need not end an ambition. It can become the reason to learn more, experiment again, and find another way forward.

Sometimes history changes because someone builds a canal. Sometimes because a television network starts a movie too early. Sometimes because a small machine begins rolling across the Moon. And sometimes because students refuse to remain silent.

And as if November 17 hadn't already accomplished enough, there's one more little milestone hiding in the date: in 1970, Douglas Engelbart received the patent for his computer pointing device—the invention that would become the computer mouse. Apparently, even the mouse wanted its moment in history. 🖱️

As for Heidi, she may have been an innocent little girl in the Swiss Alps, but American football fans have never quite forgiven her.  🤭

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

✅ QUIZ ANSWER: [B] A children's movie replaced the live broadcast before the game ended.

NBC switched from the Jets–Raiders game with 65 seconds remaining. Oakland scored twice in the final nine seconds and won 43–32. Millions of viewers missed the finish, and television broadcasting history was never quite the same.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🍬 CANDY

Tomorrow, history has another collection of surprises waiting. Somewhere between ambition and absurdity, an ordinary situation will take an extraordinary turn—and someone will discover that the past has a peculiar sense of timing.

No names. No spoilers. Just a little mystery to keep the curiosity alive.

Until then, stay curious. The next strange chapter is already waiting.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

💋 SEND-OFF

If today's stories made you smile, think, or wonder how any of this actually happened, pass them along.

Share the strange, challenge the familiar, and keep asking questions. History is far too interesting to leave sitting quietly on a shelf.

Until next time, keep your curiosity sharp—and if you're watching a football game, remember to keep an eye on the television schedule. Heidi may be waiting in the wings.

𝗥𝗨𝗡𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗕𝗔𝗖𝗞𝗦 🪙

▫️𝗞𝗲𝗻𝗻𝘆 𝗚𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘄𝗲𝗹𝗹, TB (@ DET)

Gainwell has totaled at least 76 yards in each of his last three games, averaging 101 yards during that stretch. A matchup with Detroit always has the potential to turn into a track meet.

▫️𝗞𝗮𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗻 𝗕𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗸, SF (vs. MIN)

Black has carved out a weekly role on the league's best offense. San Francisco is committed to preserving CMC, and if he misses time, Black immediately becomes a top-10 RB. He should be rostered in EVERY league.

▫️𝗦𝗲𝘁𝗵 𝗠𝗰𝗚𝗼𝘄𝗮𝗻, IND (@ HOU)

Plenty of managers dropped McGowan after Jonathan Taylor wasn't traded, but he still has a legitimate role. With the Colts potentially facing a lost season, there's a chance Taylor could be shut down late in the year.

▫️𝗝𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗛𝗶𝗹𝗹, BAL (@ CAR)

Baltimore's season hit a low point with its loss to the previously winless Chargers. 

Hill's speed and pass-catching ability are things this offense needs, and this backfield is more of a timeshare than most realize. Excellent matchup against Carolina.

𝗪𝗜𝗗𝗘 𝗥𝗘𝗖𝗘𝗜𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗦 🎯

▫️𝗧𝗿𝗲 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗶𝘀, LAC (vs. NYJ)

Ladd McConkey's injury struggles continue, and Harris is taking advantage. 

He played nearly every snap in Week 10 and accounted for 67% of the team's receiving yards. Great matchup ahead for an ascending young player.

▫️𝗣𝗮𝘁 𝗕𝗿𝘆𝗮𝗻𝘁, DEN (vs. LV)

Bryant has been effective when on the field for Denver and should be heavily involved going forward now that he's healthy again.

▫️𝗔𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗼 𝗪𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗺𝘀, WAS (vs. CIN)

Williams continues to lead Washington's receivers in snaps since Terry McLaurin went down. 

A potential shootout against Cincinnati gives him an opportunity to deliver another useful fantasy performance.

▫️𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗯 𝗗𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗹𝗮𝘀, MIA (@ BUF)

We don't care what the situation looks like when the fantasy points keep coming. Douglas has emerged as Miami's best WR and should see plenty of volume against Buffalo. 

He's topped 70 yards in three of his last four games and brings legitimate big-play ability.

𝗧𝗜𝗚𝗛𝗧 𝗘𝗡𝗗𝗦 💸

▫️𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸 𝗔𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗲𝘄𝘀, BAL (@ CAR)

Right around the 50% ownership cutoff, Andrews is a priority add if available. New Ravens QB Jacoby Brissett peppered him with targets in his debut and has historically loved targeting tight ends. Go get him!

▫️𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗲𝗹 𝗠𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿, LV (@ DEN)

Brock Bowers could miss time with an ankle injury. Mayer is already playing nearly every snap, but would become a focal point of the passing game for Fernando Mendoza if Bowers is sidelined.

▫️𝗖𝗵𝗶𝗴 𝗢𝗸𝗼𝗻𝗸𝘄𝗼, WAS (vs. CIN)

A potential shootout with Cincinnati on Monday night gives Okonkwo an opportunity. He has the big-play ability to take advantage, and the Bengals have been one of the league's worst defenses against tight ends.

𝗗𝗘𝗙𝗘𝗡𝗦𝗘 𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗠𝗘𝗥𝗦 🔒

▫️𝗦𝗮𝗻 𝗙𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼 𝟰𝟵𝗲𝗿𝘀 (vs. MIN)

Don't let last week's shootout with Dallas fool you. San Francisco has a legitimate defense and gets a Vikings offense with plenty to prove. 

The 49ers harassed Kirk Cousins just a couple of weeks ago.

▫️𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘀 (vs. NYJ)

The Chargers defense has quietly played decent football when given the opportunity. 

They get a favorable matchup against the Jets, who may be without Geno Smith, and their offense should put them in good field position.

▫️𝗟𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 (vs. TB)

Tampa Bay's passing game has been nearly nonexistent this season, and Baker Mayfield's status is uncertain. 

If Detroit can play with a lead, they could have plenty of opportunities to generate sacks and turnovers.

text:
Is there a worse contract in the NFL right now than DK Metcalf’s?

If the Steelers were to cut Metcalf today, they’d reportedly be on the hook for around $36 million.

And based on his production this season, it’s getting harder to justify that investment.

Metcalf hasn’t looked anything like a legitimate number one wide receiver. Most weeks, he’s producing more like a number two or even number three option.

His 15.4% drop rate is the worst of his career.

He dropped another pass against Cincinnati, and just two weeks earlier against Cleveland, one of his drops turned into an interception.

But here’s what really caught my attention.

Lately, we’ve seen the Steelers try to force-feed Metcalf the football late in games, often when the outcome is already decided.

So I went back and looked at his production without those garbage-time receptions.

Through nine games, here’s what you’re left with:

30 receptions. 339 receiving yards.

That’s an average of just three catches for 37 yards per game.

For a player carrying that kind of financial commitment, that’s nowhere near good enough.

The Steelers brought Metcalf in to be a difference-maker. Someone who could elevate the passing game and give Aaron Rodgers a legitimate number one target.

Instead, he’s been inconsistent, struggled with drops, and failed to deliver the production this offense desperately needs.

At some point, we have to ask whether the Steelers are getting anything close to what they’re paying for.

Because right now, I don’t think they are.
